dissent_taxonomy.notes:
All 45 has_dissent options are CFFTF (20 cfftf-final 'reform/revenue/expenditure' recs, 25 cfftf-interim). Validated 15 against the PDFs (>=10 required), including all three named A/B-split options; in every case sources.json dissent_summary preserves the true direction (direction_faithful=true for all 15).

IMPORTANT nuance on opposing_split_ids: Of the three A/B-split options the task names as 'opposing,' only TWO are genuinely opposing (too_far vs not_far_enough): institute-vacancy-freeze (p16) and increase-autonomous-drones-cpd (p30). The third, cfftf-ltl-external-funding-adc (p32-33), has two dissents but they do NOT oppose: Dissent A says targeting 100% funding (vs the 90% required by law) goes too far, and Dissent B suggests the funding-percentage target could be LOWERED — both lean toward LESS funding. sources.json correctly captures this (A=too_far, B=alternative-lower) and never claims a not_far_enough split. I list all three in opposing_split_ids because the task explicitly names them as the A/B-split set to surface, but flag here that ADC is not a genuine too_far/not_far_enough opposition. In the taxonomy I therefore classified ADC under 'Goes too far' (its dominant thrust), not under the 2-count 'Opposing dual dissents' category.

Taxonomy is direction-based (4 categories), aligning with the task's emphasis and the validated[] direction enum; counts sum to 45 (22+18+3+2).

Boundary judgments documented for transparency: (1) The cfftf-final shared 'Additional Fees, Fines & Taxes' dissent (recs 21-25, text on p60) splits into Dissent A (Springfield could enable progressive options — a not-far-enough/redirect lean), B (do cost-benefit analyses — process/caution), and C (specific to CPI property tax + sales-tax expansion — cautionary that those two overreach). I placed PPRT, LGDF, and cordon congestion pricing under 'Alternative/caution' (only A+B apply), and resume-cpi-property-tax + expand-sales-tax under 'Goes too far' (Dissent C is a substantive overreach concern). (2) graduated-income-tax and restructure-electricity-tax read as cautionary 'study business-climate impact first' so I placed them in Alternative/caution rather than too_far. (3) increase-garbage-fee and adjust-city-property-tax carry a progressive 'tax the wealthy instead' flavor but their dominant thrust is that the regressive measure overreaches/harms, so they sit in 'Goes too far.' (4) favor-natural-expiration-of-tifs: the dissent opposes prioritizing expiration and urges collaboration to fast-track infrastructure — I read this as opposing the recommendation's push (too far) rather than a pure alternative. These ~4-5 caution-vs-too-far boundary calls are inherently judgment calls; the underlying dissent_summaries are all faithful regardless of bucket.

The five CPL recs (16-20) share ONE dissent printed on p57 after rec 20; sources.json correctly attaches it to all five. The fees/taxes shared dissent on p60 is correctly distributed across recs 21-25 with the rec-specific Dissent C only on CPI and sales-tax. Page citations in the option records point to each option's recommendation page; the dissent text frequently sits on the following page (e.g., interim dissents on p16/p19/p26/p29/p30; ADC Dissent B on p33) — this is expected and consistent with the PDFs.

gap_reconcile.narrative:
All 13 figures verified verbatim on their cited printed pages (printed page = pdf_index+1 holds for all three reports). The figures genuinely disagree, but the disagreement is almost entirely about WHAT is being measured, not about errors. Four axes of divergence:

1) FISCAL YEAR. The headline numbers attach to different years. The two CFFTF Interim and EY 'big' numbers are FY2026 near-term gaps (~$1.1-1.2B). The CFFTF Final's headline $680M is a FY2027 figure. They are not the same quantity at all: $1.1-1.2B is the cyclical FY2026 hole (inflated by expiring one-time pandemic/TIF revenues), while $680M is what the Final says persists into FY2027 and beyond once those one-time effects are gone (Final p.5, p.10).

2) POINT-IN-TIME vs DURABLE/RANGE. The Final deliberately reframes the problem from a single-year gap to a durable structural gap, citing $680M as the persistent baseline (p.5) and $680-$780M as the recurring annual range (p.10). The Interim and EY are point-in-time single-year deficit forecasts.

3) RESTATEMENT / ROUNDING. The same FY2026 gap is quoted three ways. The Interim states its OWN number as '$1.1 billion' and 'over $1.1 billion' (p.7, p.10); EY independently forecasts 'roughly $1.15 billion' (p.4); and the Final, summarizing the Interim, rounds it UP to '$1.2 billion' (p.6). So the Final's $1.2B is a restatement of the Interim's $1.1B, not a fourth distinct estimate — a key reconciliation point, since a naive reader would treat $1.1B, $1.15B, and $1.2B as three different gaps when they are one gap rounded differently.

4) MEASURE / SCOPE. The FY2025 figures look contradictory but are not: the Interim's '$982.4 million' (p.10) is the PROJECTED Corporate Fund deficit before mitigation, while EY's 'approximately $146 million' (p.4) is the projected YEAR-END outturn after the city's in-year actions. Different points in the budget cycle, same year. Separately, several figures are not gaps at all: $6.5B (Final p.7) is the Corporate Fund's total size (the denominator); $35.9B (Interim p.11) is the unfunded pension LIABILITY (a balance-sheet driver, not an annual operating gap); $175M (EY p.4, CPS reimbursement) and $820M (EY p.4, cumulative supplemental pension payments since 2023) are drivers/context. EY's '$530M-$1.396B' (p.5) is the SOLUTION menu, not the gap — and notably only its high end fully covers the ~$1.15B FY2026 gap.

Reconciled picture: there is ONE near-term FY2026 Corporate Fund gap (~$1.1-1.2B, all sources agreeing within rounding) and ONE durable structural gap the Final isolates for FY2027+ ($680M, range $680-$780M). Everything else is either the same number restated, a different fiscal year, or context/liability/solution figures that should not be mistaken for the gap.

targets.basis: CFFTF Final Report p.5 ('$680 million shortfall that persists even under baseline assumptions'), reinforced by the $680-$780M annual range on p.10.
targets.implication: This is the honest long-term target: the gap that survives after one-time resources unwind. Choosing it forces the player to close the gap with RECURRING levers only (structural revenue, permanent cost reductions, pension/State action) and to disallow one-time plugs like TIF surplus or asset sales from counting toward victory. Hardest framing, but the one the Final Report treats as the real problem.
targets.name: The Durable Structural Gap (recurring-only)

targets.basis: EY p.4 ('Corporate Fund gap of roughly $1.15 billion'), corroborated by CFFTF Interim p.7/p.10 ('$1.1 billion' / 'over $1.1 billion') and the Final's restatement on p.6 ('$1.2 billion FY2026 budget gap'). A defensible point figure of ~$1.15B sits squarely inside that $1.1-1.2B band.
targets.implication: This is the immediate budget the mayor must actually balance for the year. Choosing it lets both one-time AND recurring levers count, mirroring how Chicago has historically closed gaps. The player feels the full crisis scale, but can 'win' the year with temporary fixes, setting up the structural-gap problem for later turns.
targets.name: The Near-Term Crisis Gap (FY2026 budget hole)

targets.basis: High end of CFFTF Final p.10's recurring structural gap range ($680-$780 million annually beginning in FY27).
targets.implication: A harder recurring target for players who want the worst-case economic assumptions. It implies weaker revenue growth and tests whether the player's recurring solutions hold up under stress. Bounded by EY's identified solution space (p.5, $530M-$1.396B), it remains closeable only if the player reaches well into the upper half of the available reform menu.
targets.name: The Upper Structural Stretch (pessimistic baseline)

overlap_groups.name: Special Events Cost Recovery — EY umbrella vs CFFTF Interim component rows
overlap_groups.rationale: EY's single 'Special Events Cost Recovery' row is a $6.3M (no ordinance change) to $21M (with ordinance expansion) umbrella covering CPD/CFD/DSS/CDOT recovery for parades, festivals, athletic and stadium events (EY p7-8). The CFFTF Interim decomposes the SAME special-events recovery opportunity into granular component rows: maximize CPD non-overtime recovery ($5.5M), reclaim other-personnel costs ($1.5M), reclaim non-personnel costs ($1.3M), capture athletic-event non-personnel costs ($0.6M), utilize full 1.5x overtime rate ($0.2M), reclaim non-city-parade costs ($11.9M), plus a non-priced data-tracking enabler. Banking the EY umbrella AND the Interim component rows double-counts the same recovered dollars — pick one representation. Interim component dollars ($5.5+1.5+1.3+0.6+0.2+11.9 = $21M) reconcile to EY's $21M high end, confirming they are the same pool. Note EY's own qualitative sub-rows (fire-ems-cost-recovery EY p11, tiered-fee-structure EY p12, harmonize-ordinances EY p11) are likewise internal pieces of this umbrella and must not be banked on top of it.

overlap_groups.name: Real Estate / Asset Monetization — CFFTF Final qualitative vs Interim grouping vs EY granular rows
overlap_groups.rationale: Three representations of monetizing the same City real-estate assets. (1) CFFTF Final 'Inventory and Monetize Non-Core Assets with Oversight' (p36) is the qualitative parent recommendation (no dollar). (2) CFFTF Interim 'Optimize the City's Real Estate Portfolio' (p61) is a single priced grouping = $29.5M Year-1 revenue, and its own text bundles 'strategic consolidation, disposition, and redevelopment... consolidate occupancy, sell properties, exit leases and renegotiate revenue generating leases' plus centralizing governance — i.e., exactly the EY granular rows. (3) EY breaks the same portfolio into granular rows totalling the Real Estate workstream of $157M-$202M (EY p6): office consolidation ($23.5-55.5M), sell vacated office buildings ($16.3-29.1M), sell industrial/non-office buildings ($57.9M), Riverwalk concession revenue-share ($13.3M), accelerated land dispositions ($45.8M), and governance/data/leasing reforms (enabler). These act on the same buildings, land parcels and leases, so banking across the three layers double-counts. (Note timeframes differ — Interim $29.5M is Year-1; EY figures are 10-year present values — but they monetize the same assets, so they remain mutually exclusive.)
